title: What is the reason for the lack of cool evolved stars near the center of the Galaxy?
comment: Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 405: Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time
summary: The observed deficit of bright late-type giants in the central parsec of the Milky Way remains an open problem. We investigate whether repeated passages of red giants (RGs) through a past jet from Sgr$~$A$^*$ can modify their envelopes and apparent spectral types. Three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations follow a $1\,M_\odot$, $100\,R_\odot$ RG through up to ten jet crossings at $10^{-3}\,\text{pc}$, using jet kinetic luminosities of $10^{42}$, $10^{44}$, and $10^{48}\,\text{erg}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Each passage produces shocks, envelope ablation, and an asymmetric downstream tail. For jet luminosities up to $10^{44}\,\text{erg}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, the cumulative ablated mass evolves approximately as $ΔM\propto t^{1/2}$ and reaches about $10^{-4}\,M_\odot$ over a $10^5\,\text{yr}$ active phase. Repeated heating also raises the surface temperature from about $3600$ to $8500\,\text{K}$ during the first ten passages, potentially making an M-type giant appear as an A-type source. Jet feedback may therefore contribute to the apparent depletion of cool giants and the excess of hot stars in galactic nuclei (GN).

AI.tldr: Hydrodynamical simulations show that repeated passages of red giants through a past jet from Sgr A* can ablate their envelopes and raise their surface temperatures from ~3600 K to ~8500 K, potentially transforming M-type giants into apparent A-type sources, which may help explain the deficit of bright late-type giants in the Galactic center.
AI.motivation: The observed deficit of bright late-type giants in the central parsec of the Milky Way remains an unsolved problem; the authors propose jet feedback as a possible explanation for this apparent depletion of cool giants.
AI.method: Three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations follow a 1 M_sun, 100 R_sun red giant through up to ten jet crossings at 10^-3 pc, using jet kinetic luminosities of 10^42, 10^44, and 10^48 erg/s. The simulations track envelope ablation, shock formation, and surface temperature evolution across multiple passages.
AI.result: Each jet passage produces shocks, envelope ablation, and an asymmetric downstream tail. For jet luminosities up to 10^44 erg/s, cumulative ablated mass scales approximately as ΔM ∝ t^1/2, reaching ~10^-4 M_sun over a 10^5 yr active phase. Surface temperature rises from ~3600 K to ~8500 K during the first ten passages.
AI.conclusion: Jet feedback may contribute to the apparent depletion of cool giants and the excess of hot stars in galactic nuclei, as repeated jet passages can make M-type giants appear as A-type sources.

title: Constraining gamma-ray burst viewing angles with Swift/XRT afterglow light curves
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the universe, and their afterglow light curves encode information about jet geometry and viewing angle. To constrain GRB viewing angles, we analyzed jet break features in Swift X-Ray Telescope afterglow light curves using two top-hat jet models: a simplified geometric model without high-latitude emission (model 1) and a comprehensive model including it (model 2). Both models were applied to a sample of 20 GRBs in an interstellar medium (ISM) and 20 in a wind medium, selected so that jet breaks are attributed to the edge effect with sufficient data coverage, and fitted with Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. We examined viewing angles and off-axis ratios q = $θ_{\rm obs}/θ_{\rm jet}$ under both density profiles, evaluating the impact of high-latitude emission. Based on reduced chi-squared and Bayesian information criterion comparisons, model 1 fits all GRBs better. Most GRBs have small off-axis ratios (mean q = 0.1851 for model 1), indicating viewing angles generally close to the jet axis; the log-space viewing-angle distribution is approximately Gaussian. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shows no significant difference in off-axis ratios between ISM and wind media, nor between bursts with and without an X-ray plateau. While viewing angles decrease significantly with redshift, the off-axis ratio shows no significant evolution, consistent with off-axis alignment being independent of cosmic epoch.

AI.tldr: The paper constrains GRB viewing angles by fitting jet break features in Swift XRT afterglow light curves using two top-hat jet models (with and without high-latitude emission) applied to 20 ISM and 20 wind medium GRBs via MCMC. Most bursts show small off-axis ratios (mean q=0.185), viewing angles decrease with redshift but off-axis ratios show no cosmic evolution, and the simpler geometric model fits data better overall.
AI.motivation: GRB afterglow light curves encode information about jet geometry and viewing angle, which are crucial for understanding jet structure, prompt emission physics, and potential gravitational wave counterparts. Constraining viewing angles helps reveal whether GRBs are observed on- or off-axis, informing models of jet energetics and unified pictures of GRB populations.
AI.method: Two top-hat jet models were applied: a simplified geometric model without high-latitude emission (model 1) and a comprehensive model including it (model 2). Both were fit to 20 GRBs in an ISM and 20 in a wind medium using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, selecting events where jet breaks arise from the edge effect with adequate data coverage. Model comparison used reduced chi-squared and Bayesian information criterion; off-axis ratios and viewing-angle distributions were statistically analyzed including Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests.
AI.result: Model 1 fits all GRBs better based on reduced chi-squared and BIC. Most GRBs have small off-axis ratios (mean q=0.1851 for model 1), implying near-jet-axis viewing angles, with approximately Gaussian log-space viewing-angle distribution. KS tests show no significant ISM vs wind difference nor plateau vs non-plateau difference in off-axis ratios. Viewing angles decrease significantly with redshift, but off-axis ratios show no significant evolution.
AI.conclusion: Simple top-hat jet models without high-latitude emission adequately describe jet breaks, GRBs are predominantly observed near the jet axis, and the alignment of observers relative to the jet axis is independent of cosmic epoch even though absolute viewing angles evolve with redshift (likely due to redshift-dependent selection effects).

title: Is the mysterious {\it Punctum} a primordial black hole?
summary: A recent study has discovered a highly polarized millimeter continuum source called {\it Punctum} located at the central region of NGC 4945 which doesn't fit any known category. Apart from the radio detection at $\approx 100$ GHz, there is no identified counterpart to {\it Punctum} in other radio, infra-red, optical, and X-ray bands. All available potential models, including magnetar, supernova remnant and microquasar, cannot provide satisfactory explanation for the exceptionally high polarization of $\sim 50$\% and large luminosity in mm band $L_{\rm mm} \approx 2\times 10^{35}$ erg/s within a small size $<2$ pc shown in {\it Punctum}. In this article, we discuss the possibility that {\it Punctum} is indeed a primordial black hole (PBH) with a dark matter density spike. We show that the synchrotron radiation due to the electrons and positrons produced from dark matter annihilation can satisfactorily explain the observed properties of {\it Punctum} and we can effectively obtain the annihilation cross section $\langle σv \rangle \sim 10^{-33}$ cm$^3$/s using our developed analytic framework. Furthermore, if the {\it Punctum} PBH mass is $\sim 10-100M_{\odot}$, the preferred dark matter mass range is $m_{\rm DM} \sim 10-1000$ MeV.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that Punctum, an unexplained highly polarized millimeter source in NGC 4945, may be a primordial black hole (PBH) surrounded by a dark matter density spike, where synchrotron radiation from dark matter annihilation products can explain its observed properties.
AI.motivation: Punctum is a newly discovered millimeter continuum source in the center of NGC 4945 that defies classification—it shows exceptionally high polarization (~50%), high mm luminosity (~2x10^35 erg/s), small size (<2 pc), and has no counterpart in other wavelengths. Existing models (magnetar, supernova remnant, microquasar) fail to explain it, motivating a new physical explanation.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytic framework to model a PBH with a dark matter density spike, calculating the synchrotron radiation emitted by electrons and positrons produced from dark matter annihilation around the PBH to compare against Punctum's observed properties.
AI.result: The synchrotron emission from dark matter annihilation products can satisfactorily explain Punctum's observed properties, yielding an annihilation cross section of ~10^-33 cm^3/s. For a PBH mass of ~10-100 M_sun, the preferred dark matter mass range is ~10-1000 MeV.
AI.conclusion: Punctum may be a primordial black hole with a dark matter density spike, providing a novel and viable explanation for this enigmatic source and potentially offering evidence for PBHs as dark matter candidates.

title: Energy-dependent extension of the Crab Nebula as a diagnostic of ultrahigh-energy hadronic emission
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Published in Physical Review D
summary: The energy-dependent apparent extension of the Crab Nebula, inconsistent with leptonic expectations between X-ray and TeV bands, can be naturally accounted for in a spatially resolved lepto-hadronic scenario. A transition to hadronic dominance occurs above $\sim400~\rm{TeV}$, with nearly pure hadronic emission at PeV energies. The predicted $68\%$ containment radius at $1.1~\rm{PeV}$ is $\sim1.4'$, about six times larger than in purely leptonic scenarios. This energy-dependent extension therefore provides an observable discriminator of the origin of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emission in pulsar wind nebulae, offering a diagnostic of PeV hadronic acceleration in the Crab Nebula.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a spatially resolved lepto-hadronic model for the Crab Nebula that explains its energy-dependent apparent extension. Hadronic emission dominates above ~400 TeV, and at PeV energies the nebula appears ~6 times more extended than in purely leptonic models, providing an observable test for PeV hadronic acceleration.
AI.motivation: The Crab Nebula's observed apparent extension between X-ray and TeV bands is inconsistent with leptonic emission expectations, suggesting an alternative (hadronic) contribution that has not been adequately explored in spatially resolved frameworks.
AI.method: A spatially resolved lepto-hadronic scenario is constructed to model the Crab Nebula, tracking the energy-dependent containment radius of emission and the transition between leptonic and hadronic contributions across energy bands.
AI.result: The model predicts a transition to hadronic dominance above ~400 TeV, with nearly pure hadronic emission at PeV energies. The predicted 68% containment radius at 1.1 PeV is ~1.4 arcminutes, about six times larger than in purely leptonic scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The energy-dependent apparent extension of the Crab Nebula serves as an observable discriminator between leptonic and hadronic origins of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emission, offering a diagnostic for PeV hadronic acceleration in pulsar wind nebulae.

title: SMUDGes Below the Surface: Clusters Confirm the Diversity of Low-Surface-Brightness Galaxies
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 26 pages, 13 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We use spatially resolved Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy to study high-surface-brightness stellar components and internal kinematics in 44 low-surface-brightness galaxies from the SMUDGes survey, including 30 ultradiffuse galaxies, spanning the red sequence, green valley, and blue cloud regions of the galaxy color-magnitude diagram. Although these galaxies appear largely smooth in survey imaging, we detect at least one cluster candidate in every galaxy. We identify clusters with nebular emission lines in 24 galaxies. They are common in blue-cloud galaxies but rare in red sequence galaxies. We identify three nuclear star cluster candidates, one of which shows nebular emission lines. Among clusters without nebular emission lines, bluer galaxies tend to have brighter cluster luminosity functions, suggesting the presence of young or intermediate-age clusters in addition to old globular clusters. This age diversity may complicate the use of photometrically selected globular cluster populations as tracers of total halo mass. We measure rotation velocities for 17 galaxies using the clusters with nebular emission lines and for 12 using diffuse stellar light. Within 0.5 effective radii, the inferred dynamical mass generally exceeds the stellar mass, although the inferred dark matter contribution varies by an order of magnitude. The variety in properties for this sample of ultradiffuse galaxies and low-surface-brightness dwarfs suggests that no single formation mechanism explains the population of low-surface-brightness galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents spatially resolved Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy of 44 low-surface-brightness galaxies (including 30 ultradiffuse galaxies) from the SMUDGes survey, detecting cluster candidates in every galaxy, nebular emission-line clusters in 24 galaxies, measuring rotation velocities for 17-12 galaxies, and finding that the diversity of properties suggests no single formation mechanism explains low-surface-brightness galaxies.
AI.motivation: To understand the nature of low-surface-brightness galaxies and ultradiffuse galaxies by studying their stellar components, internal kinematics, and cluster populations, which are poorly constrained compared to normal galaxies.
AI.method: Using spatially resolved Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy to study 44 low-surface-brightness galaxies from the SMUDGes survey, detecting star clusters, identifying those with nebular emission lines, measuring cluster luminosity functions, and deriving rotation velocities and dynamical masses.
AI.result: All 44 galaxies contain at least one cluster candidate; 24 show nebular emission-line clusters (common in blue-cloud, rare in red-sequence galaxies); three nuclear star cluster candidates identified; bluer galaxies have brighter cluster luminosity functions; rotation velocities measured for 17 galaxies (via clusters) and 12 (via diffuse light); dynamical mass exceeds stellar mass within 0.5 effective radii, but dark matter contribution varies by an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The wide variety in properties across this sample suggests that no single formation mechanism can explain the population of low-surface-brightness galaxies, and the age diversity in cluster populations may complicate using globular clusters as total halo mass tracers.

title: A Population Study for Searching Supermassive Binary Black Holes in Active Galactic Nuclei: Continuum Spectral Features and Periodic Variabilities
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures
summary: Active sub-pc supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) are expected to exhibit various electromagnetic signatures due to unique dynamical and geometric structures of their accretion, but observational identification of them remains challenging. In this paper, we adopt semianalytic models to investigate both deficits in spectral-energy-distributions (SEDs) of these systems induced by gaps/holes in their accretion disks and periodic variations in their light curves induced by either orbital-modulated Doppler boosting or accretion rate variation of each SMBH component. We construct a population model to generate SMBBHs across cosmic time by considering their orbital evolution and associated accretion and radiation processes. By estimating the continuum emission from each mock system and its variation, we investigate the detection of SMBBHs via either SED-deficit signature or light curve periodicity under reasonably given criteria. We find that all-sky surveys with filters similar to those of the China Space Station Telescope or Rubin/LSST could identify up to approximately $3\times 10^2$ SMBBHs via SED-deficit features and/or $10^3$ SMBBHs via periodicity ($\lesssim5$\,yr), although both selections may suffer from a high rate of false positives. A few to a dozen SED-deficit SMBBHs may be detected by future pulsar timing arrays with signal-to-noise ratio $\gtrsim3$, enabling multi-messenger observations. Only $\sim20\%-53\%$ of SED-deficit selected SMBBHs may also be detected via periodic variations, and $\sim7\%-9\%$ of periodic variation selected SMBBHs may be detected via SED-deficit signatures. The false positives for those SMBBHs selected jointly by both methods are negligible, highlighting the importance of searching for active SMBBH systems using joint methods.

AI.tldr: This paper develops semianalytic models and a cosmic population model to predict detection rates of active supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) via two observational signatures: SED deficits from accretion disk gaps/holes and periodic light curve variations from orbital Doppler boosting or accretion rate modulation. All-sky surveys (CSST or Rubin/LSST) could identify ~3×10² SMBBHs via SED deficits and ~10³ via periodicity (≤5 yr), though with high false-positive rates. Joint selection by both methods yields negligible false positives, and a few to a dozen SED-deficit SMBBHs may be detectable by future pulsar timing arrays for multi-messenger observations.
AI.motivation: Observational identification of active supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) remains challenging despite predictions of distinct electromagnetic signatures from their unique accretion dynamics and geometry. This paper aims to quantify how many SMBBHs can be detected via SED-deficit and periodic-variation signatures using future surveys and multi-messenger facilities.
AI.method: The authors (1) adopt semianalytic models to characterize SED deficits from accretion disk gaps/holes and periodic light curve variations from orbital-modulated Doppler boosting or accretion rate variation; (2) construct a population model generating SMBBHs across cosmic time with orbital evolution, accretion, and radiation processes; (3) simulate continuum emission for each mock system; (4) apply detection criteria for both SED-deficit and periodicity signatures, including false-positive assessments, and evaluate joint detection and cross-matching with pulsar timing arrays.
AI.result: All-sky surveys with CSST-like or Rubin/LSST-like filters could detect up to ~3×10² SMBBHs via SED-deficit features and ~10³ via periodic variations (≤5 yr), though both suffer high false positives. A few to a dozen SED-deficit SMBBHs may be detected by future pulsar timing arrays with SNR≥3. Only ~20%–53% of SED-deficit-selected SMBBHs also show periodic variations, and ~7%–9% of periodicity-selected SMBBHs show SED deficits. Joint selection by both methods yields negligible false positives.
AI.conclusion: Joint detection using both SED-deficit and periodic-variation signatures is essential for robustly identifying active SMBBHs, with negligible false positives when both methods agree. The relatively low overlap between the two selections underscores that each method probes complementary subpopulations, and the combination with pulsar timing arrays enables promising multi-messenger opportunities.

title: The ionizing properties of JWST's compact broad-line emitters
comment: Main text 19 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: The recent JWST discovery of a numerous population of broad-line emitters (BLEs) at $z>4$ has reopened the question of whether sources other than faint galaxies contributed significantly to cosmic reionization. To assess this contribution, we present a systematic census of compact, blue broad-line emitters at $4\leq z\leq7$ selected from the DJA, designed to isolate sources in which the UV continuum and the broad-line emission originate from the same compact physical region. Starting from a parent sample of 4145 galaxies with NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy and NIRCam imaging, we apply criteria on broad Ha emission (FWHM$>2000$km s-1, detected at S/N$\geq5$, complete at $L_{Ha,broad}\geq10^{42.7}$erg s-1), blue continuum slopes ($β_{UV}\leq-1.5$, $β_{opt}<0.5$), and morphological compactness in both the rest-frame UV and optical, returning a final sample of 20 sources. This constitutes $\sim20%$ of the PRISM-selected broad-line sample, which is dominated by Little Red Dots (LRDs). We find that the compact blue BLEs display hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines (CIV, NIV], HeII), and elevated Lya emitter fractions ($X_{Lya}=50-67%$) relative to star-forming galaxies and LRDs. Beyond their similar lack of X-ray emission, their optical spectra closely resemble those of LRDs. This suggests that compact blue BLEs extend this population towards lower column density envelopes, but with similar engines, rather than representing a physically distinct population. Using Sirocco to model physical configurations that reproduce the observed spectra, we find a high ionizing photon production efficiency (log$ξ_{ion}\sim25.4$Hz erg-1) and a weighted average escape fraction $fesc\sim0.2$ for the bluest sources, and $\sim0.01$ for LRDs. This implies that broad-line sources do not dominate reionization globally, but given their luminosity, their contribution can dominate up to few Mpc scales.

AI.tldr: A census of 20 compact, blue broad-line emitters at 4≤z≤7 from the DJA (NIRSpec/PRISM + NIRCam) reveals they are an extension of the Little Red Dots population with lower column density envelopes, sharing similar central engines. Using Sirocco spectral modeling, they exhibit high ionizing photon production efficiency (log ξion ~25.4 Hz erg⁻¹) and escape fraction ~0.2 for bluest sources (~0.01 for LRDs), suggesting broad-line sources do not dominate reionization globally but can dominate on few Mpc scales.
AI.motivation: The recent JWST discovery of numerous broad-line emitters at z>4 reopens the question of whether non-galactic sources (e.g., AGN-like compact objects) contributed significantly to cosmic reionization, motivating a systematic assessment of their ionizing photon production and escape.
AI.method: From a parent sample of 4145 galaxies with NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy and NIRCam imaging, the authors applied selection criteria including broad Hα emission (FWHM>2000 km/s, S/N≥5, complete at L≥10^42.7 erg/s), blue continuum slopes (β_UV≤−1.5, β_opt<0.5), and morphological compactness in rest-frame UV and optical, yielding 20 compact blue BLEs. Spectral properties were compared to LRDs and star-forming galaxies, and Sirocco photoionization modeling was used to constrain ionizing photon production efficiency and escape fractions.
AI.result: The 20 compact blue BLEs (~20% of the PRISM-selected broad-line sample) show hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines (CIV, NIV], HeII), and elevated Lyα emitter fractions (50–67%) compared to star-forming galaxies and LRDs. Their optical spectra resemble LRDs and lack X-ray emission. Sirocco modeling yields log ξion~25.4 Hz erg⁻¹ and fesc~0.2 for bluest sources, ~0.01 for LRDs.
AI.conclusion: Compact blue BLEs are not a physically distinct population but represent the low-column-density extension of LRDs with similar central engines. Broad-line sources do not dominate cosmic reionization globally, but their contribution can be locally dominant on scales up to a few Mpc given their luminosity.

title: Energy Partition in AGN-driven Bubbles of NGC 4438: From Nuclear Bubbles to a Galaxy-scale Outflow
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, Accepted by ApJ, comments welcome
summary: Jets launched by accreting supermassive black holes represent a major mode of active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback. However, how their energy is divided among bulk kinetic motion, thermal gas, magnetic fields, cosmic rays (CRs), and radiation - and how this distribution changes with spatial scale - remains poorly constrained. NGC 4438 provides a unique laboratory for probing this evolution, hosting two 200-pc-scale nuclear bubbles and a lopsided ~10 kpc galaxy-scale outflow plausibly associated with the same AGN. We present a multi-wavelength analysis to investigate the morphology, radiation mechanisms, and energetics of these structures. Joint radio-X-ray modeling shows that the non-thermal emission in the nuclear bubbles may require two distinct populations of cosmic-ray electrons, suggesting that in addition to shock acceleration at the bubble rim, the highest-energy particles may be linked to acceleration processes closer to the unresolved central engine. A spatially resolved energy inventory reveals that bulk kinetic energy dominates the current energy budget of the nuclear bubbles, while roughly half of the injected energy has already been transformed into thermal, CR, and magnetic energy, as well as radiative losses. Across all bubble sizes, the thermal and magnetic pressures are consistent within the uncertainties, implying that magnetic fields remain dynamically significant on all examined spatial scales. Furthermore, the empirical correlation between radio luminosity and jet power, established for kiloparsec-scale jet bubbles (MerloniHeinz2007), matches the energetics of the galaxy-scale outflow but substantially overestimates the power of the 200-pc-scale nuclear bubbles, underscoring the scale dependence of jet energy dissipation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-wavelength analysis of NGC 4438, which hosts both 200-pc-scale nuclear bubbles and a ~10 kpc galaxy-scale outflow from AGN jet feedback. The authors find that bulk kinetic energy dominates the nuclear bubbles' energy budget, two cosmic-ray electron populations are needed to explain the radio-X-ray emission, and that the jet power-scaling relation for kpc-scale bubbles overestimates the power of the smaller nuclear bubbles.
AI.motivation: The energy partition of AGN jets—among kinetic, thermal, magnetic, cosmic ray, and radiative components—and how it evolves with spatial scale is poorly constrained. NGC 4438 offers a unique opportunity because it hosts both small nuclear bubbles and a large galaxy-scale outflow likely from the same AGN, enabling a scale-dependent study of jet energetics.
AI.method: The authors perform a multi-wavelength analysis (radio to X-ray) to characterize the morphology, radiation mechanisms, and energetics of the nuclear bubbles and galaxy-scale outflow. They use joint radio-X-ray spectral modeling to constrain non-thermal emission processes and construct a spatially resolved energy inventory of the bubbles.
AI.result: Two distinct cosmic-ray electron populations are required to explain the nuclear bubble non-thermal emission, suggesting both rim shock acceleration and processes nearer the central engine. Bulk kinetic energy dominates the current bubble energy budget, with ~half of injected energy converted to thermal, CR, magnetic, and radiative forms. Thermal and magnetic pressures are comparable at all scales. The Merloni-Heinz radio luminosity–jet power relation matches the galaxy-scale outflow but overestimates the nuclear bubble power by a significant margin.
AI.conclusion: The energy dissipation of AGN jets is strongly scale-dependent: smaller (200-pc) bubbles dissipate a larger fraction of their energy while being energetically overestimated by standard jet-power scaling relations derived at kpc scales. Magnetic fields remain dynamically important across all spatial scales examined, and multiple acceleration mechanisms are likely operating in the nuclear region.

title: To be lensed or not to be lensed: on the nature of the alleged high-z lensed quasars J0109-5424 and P170+20
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal, 10 pages, 4 figures
summary: We present a detailed multi-wavelength analysis of two gravitationally lensed z>6 quasar candidates: J0109-5424 and P170+20. Using JWST/NIRSpec near-infrared data from the Aether survey, we demonstrate that J0109-5424 is in fact a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07, exhibiting strong iron broad absorption lines that mimic the Lyman break. From the Pabeta emission line, we estimate a black hole mass of 3.9 x 10^8 Msun and a bolometric luminosity of Lbol = 7.7 x 10^45 erg/s for this quasar. Follow-up HST/ACS WFC imaging of P170+20 with the F555W filter, probing emission below the Lyman limit of the quasar, reveals a compact source located 0.09+/-0.04 arcsec from the quasar position. PSF modelling and subtraction yield no evidence for extended emission. This is inconsistent with a foreground galaxy acting as a lens. Furthermore, we obtain Gemini-South/Flamingos 2 near-infrared observations to complement the existing optical Gemini-North/GMOS spectrum of P170+20. Our spectral analysis shows that the observed spectral shape of P170+20 is consistent with a composite quasar and M-dwarf spectrum. However, this interpretation remains uncertain, as a chance alignment between an ultracool dwarf and a quasar within 0.1 arcsec would be unlikely. Overall, our findings establish J0109-5424 as an intermediate redshift source and do not favor the lensed nature of P170+20, although this possibility cannot be conclusively ruled out, highlighting the challenges of selecting lensed quasars at high redshift.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-wavelength analysis of two candidate lensed z>6 quasars. J0109-5424 is reclassified as a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07 with strong iron absorption mimicking the Lyman break, harboring a ~3.9×10^8 Msun black hole. P170+20 shows no evidence of a foreground lensing galaxy in deep HST imaging, and its spectrum is consistent with a quasar plus M-dwarf composite, making its lensed nature unlikely but not conclusively ruled out.
AI.motivation: To verify the nature of two gravitationally lensed z>6 quasar candidates and address the challenges and potential contaminants in selecting high-redshift lensed quasars, which are important cosmological probes but can be mimicked by lower-redshift objects or chance alignments.
AI.method: The authors use JWST/NIRSpec near-infrared spectroscopy from the Aether survey to classify J0109-5424, measuring its emission lines (Pabeta) to estimate black hole mass and bolometric luminosity. For P170+20, they use HST/ACS WFC imaging (F555W) with PSF modelling to search for lensing galaxy emission, and Gemini-South/Flamingos 2 NIR spectroscopy combined with existing Gemini-North/GMOS optical data for spectral decomposition.
AI.result: J0109-5424 is a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07 with M_BH = 3.9×10^8 Msun and Lbol = 7.7×10^45 erg/s. For P170+20, HST imaging reveals a compact source 0.09±0.04 arcsec from the quasar with no extended emission, inconsistent with a foreground lensing galaxy. The spectral shape is consistent with a composite quasar and M-dwarf spectrum, though the required close alignment is statistically unlikely.
AI.conclusion: Neither source is confirmed as a genuine lensed z>6 quasar: J0109-5424 is an intermediate-redshift FeLoBAL quasar, and P170+20's lensed nature is not favored (though not fully excluded). This demonstrates that high-redshift lensed quasar selection is prone to contamination from spectral mimics and requires careful multi-wavelength follow-up.

title: Weak gravitational lensing by a dark-matter-admixed neutron star: a self-consistent two-fluid halo and the Gauss--Bonnet deflection angle
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: We compute the weak gravitational deflection of light by a neutron star that carries a self-consistent dark-matter component, in the regime in which the dark matter forms an "extended halo" reaching beyond the baryonic surface. Two observations motivate this configuration. First, a dark-matter core confined within the baryonic radius leaves no distinctive lensing signature, since by Birkhoff's theorem the exterior is Schwarzschild with the total mass, so a ray passing outside the star feels only that mass and the compactness it implies. Second, the signature we seek resides in the complementary case, in which the ray genuinely traverses the halo, so that the surrounding density enters the optical geometry directly. We model the star by integrating the coupled two-fluid Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff equations, with the baryonic and dark components interacting solely through gravity, and we obtain the deflection angle from the resulting external profile through the Gibbons--Werner construction of the Gauss--Bonnet theorem. The defining feature of the approach is that the deflection is tied to a "self-consistent" two-fluid profile rather than to a medium inserted by hand. We show that, for impact parameters smaller than the halo radius, the deflection departs measurably from the point-mass prediction, the deficit being governed by the dark-matter fraction and the halo extent, and we argue that the "shape" of this deficit furnishes a geometric, lensing-based handle on the degeneracy between dark matter and the nuclear equation of state. The framework thereby unites the structural modelling of compact stars with their gravitational-lensing phenomenology.

AI.tldr: The paper computes weak gravitational deflection of light by neutron stars with self-consistent dark-matter halos, using a two-fluid TOV model and the Gibbons-Werner Gauss-Bonnet method, showing that rays traversing the halo produce a measurable deflection deficit governed by dark-matter fraction and halo extent, offering a lensing-based probe to break the degeneracy between dark matter and the nuclear equation of state.
AI.motivation: Two key observations motivate this work: (1) A dark-matter core confined within the baryonic radius leaves no distinctive lensing signature due to Birkhoff's theorem (exterior is Schwarzschild with total mass), and (2) the sought signature resides in the complementary case where dark matter forms an "extended halo" beyond the baryonic surface, so rays genuinely traverse the halo and the density enters the optical geometry directly.
AI.method: The authors model the neutron star by integrating the coupled two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations, with baryonic and dark components interacting only through gravity. They obtain the deflection angle from the resulting external density profile using the Gibbons-Werner construction based on the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.
AI.result: For impact parameters smaller than the halo radius, the deflection departs measurably from the point-mass prediction. The deficit is governed by the dark-matter fraction and the halo extent. The "shape" of this deficit provides a geometric, lensing-based handle on the degeneracy between dark matter and the nuclear equation of state.
AI.conclusion: The framework unites the structural modelling of compact stars with their gravitational-lensing phenomenology, demonstrating that a self-consistent two-fluid profile (rather than a medium inserted by hand) yields distinctive, measurable lensing signatures that can serve as a probe of dark matter in neutron star environments.

title: Tracing Galaxy Bias Through the Cosmic Web: The Role of Filaments
comment: Submitted to A&A, 14 pages, 13 figures
summary: The large-scale clustering of galaxies depends not only on their internal properties but also on their location within the cosmic web, which defines the anisotropic environments where galaxies form and evolve. Filaments serve as bridges through which galaxies and dark matter flow from low-density regions toward the highest-density nodes. In this work, we aim to map galaxy bias, which quantifies how these tracers follow the underlying dark matter density field, through the cosmic web, with a special emphasis on filaments. We look for dependencies on filament properties, such as length and density, and characterize the spatial variations of the large-scale bias along the filamentary spine. We applied the DisPerSE algorithm to identify the cosmic web in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulation. To measure large-scale galaxy bias, we utilized an object-by-object estimator, which provides advantages over standard estimators. We find that galaxies in node outskirts exhibit the highest large-scale bias values, reaching up to $\sim4$ times the values expected from theoretical models based on halo mass alone. Low-mass red galaxies in filaments and filament outskirts also display enhanced bias, which is strongly reduced after excluding galaxies close to nodes. Together, these results suggest that proximity to massive nodes plays a central role in shaping environmental secondary bias. Furthermore, galaxy bias decreases with filament length, from mean values of $1.4$ for short filaments to $-0.5$ for longer structures. This relation persists at fixed halo mass and galaxy color, and is not primarily driven by the average local galaxy density of the filament. Finally, short filaments exhibit an approximately uniform longitudinal bias profile, whereas long filaments show an increase in normalized bias from $\sim0.85$ near the saddle point to $\sim1.06$ close to the node.

AI.method: The DisPerSE algorithm was applied to identify cosmic web structures in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulation. An object-by-object estimator was used to measure large-scale galaxy bias, preferred over standard estimators.

title: Ultraluminous X-ray sources in the first eROSITA survey I. Candidate catalogs
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, in press in Astronomy and Astrophysics, volume 712
summary: Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are luminous non-nuclear X-ray point sources embedded in galaxies. Their luminosities exceeding 10^39 erg/s potentially require sub-Eddington accretion by objects with masses from ~10^2$M_{\odot}$ to ~10^4$M_{\odot}$ or supercritical accretion beyond the Eddington limit by stellar mass black holes or neutron stars. We identified ULXs by searching for X-ray counterparts in the ~10^5 galaxies of the HECATE catalog in the footprint of the first eROSITA all-sky survey, while excluding nuclear regions to avoid the selection of active galactic nuclei (AGN). We characterized the completeness of the sample and its contamination by unidentified AGN and determined the influence of source confusion. The catalog is unaffected by X-ray selection biases. We removed known contaminants such as supernovae, stars, and AGN, and manually vetted all candidates to further remove contaminants. We derived the X-ray selection function and fraction of unidentified AGN interlopers using a simulation with subsequent source detection. We present two samples of ULX candidates. The main sample consists of 90 sources with highly confident X-ray detections, 53 of which are identified for the first time. This sample is complete to a distance of ~7Mpc, contains at most 29% of unknown background AGN, and is mostly unaffected by source confusion. Several candidates are newly identified even though their locations have been observed by other instruments before, and some previously reported candidates we expected to identify are absent from our sample, demonstrating the transient behavior of ULXs. Based on our list of less confident detections, we also provide an extended catalog of 260 sources identified as potential candidates for further ULX identifications. Of these, 245 are identified as potential candidates for the first time. (Abridged)

title: A systematic study of AGN feedback in a disk galaxy using MACER. III. High Gas Fractions in AGN Hosts
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures. To be submitted to ApJ
summary: We use high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations in the MACER framework to explain why low-redshift PG quasar hosts can retain substantial cold-gas reservoirs, with gas fractions and gas-to-stellar mass ratios showing little dependence on instantaneous AGN luminosity. This paper is the third in a series systematically studying AGN feedback in a disk galaxy subject to cosmological gas inflow. The simulations include multiphase gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and self-consistent radiative and mechanical AGN feedback. We reproduce the observed weak connection between host-galaxy gas content and AGN luminosity over L_AGN/L_Edd ~ 10^{-5}-10, while the galaxy nevertheless undergoes pronounced gas depletion and star-formation quenching. During the quenching phase, the cold-gas mass declines by nearly three orders of magnitude, and the evolution of the gas distribution shows that AGN feedback progressively removes both cold and hot gas from the galaxy. The star formation rate is more closely linked to the cold-gas mass than to AGN luminosity. This behavior arises from a timescale mismatch: AGN luminosity varies on ~ 10^5-10^6 yr timescales, whereas repeated AGN-driven outflows cumulatively deplete the galaxy-scale gas reservoir over ~ 1 Gyr. Our simulations therefore provide a physical explanation for the gas-rich PG quasar hosts and show that their observed gas properties are fully consistent with effective, long-term ejective AGN feedback.

AI.method: High-resolution hydrodynamic simulations within the MACER framework, including multiphase gas treatment, star formation, stellar feedback, and self-consistent radiative and mechanical AGN feedback, applied to a disk galaxy with cosmological gas inflow.

title: The properties of the first continuous gravitational waves: Optimizing pulsar timing observations for supermassive black hole binary detection
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 23 pages, 14 figures
summary: Several pulsar timing arrays have reported evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background. This background is thought to arise from the superposition of signals from a population of inspiraling supermassive black hole binaries. A key test of this interpretation is the search for individually resolvable binaries whose signals emerge above this background. Here we investigate this possibility by addressing two related questions: (1) what are the most probable properties of the first resolvable binary; and (2) how can pulsar timing observations be optimized to maximize its prospects for electromagnetic identification? By simulating populations of supermassive black hole binaries constrained by evidence for the gravitational-wave background and studying the loudest binary in each simulation, we infer the expected properties of the first individually resolvable systems. If MeerKAT continues its current observing strategy for a total of 9 years, the probability of detecting an individual binary is $\approx10-27\%$. Improving the timing precision by a factor of two changes this probability to $\approx11-28\%$, whereas increasing the cadence by a factor of four gives $\approx12-30\%$. Combining both improvements yields a detection probability of $\approx12-33\%$. Furthermore, implementing a high-cadence observing campaign preferentially resolves higher-frequency systems ($\gtrsim\unit[10]{nHz}$), whose shorter orbital periods make them considerably easier to identify through electromagnetic observations than lower-frequency binaries that repeat infrequently. We discuss prospects of electromagnetic follow-up of gravitational-wave resolved binaries with current high-cadence all-sky optical surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the properties and detection prospects of the first individually resolvable supermassive black hole binaries in pulsar timing array data, finding that with current MeerKAT observing strategies the detection probability is ~10-27%, and that optimized observing strategies (particularly high-cadence campaigns) improve detection odds and preferentially resolve higher-frequency binaries that are easier to identify electromagnetically.
AI.motivation: Pulsar timing arrays have detected a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, which is hypothesized to arise from supermassive black hole binaries. A key test of this interpretation is detecting individually resolvable binaries that emerge above the background, motivating the question of what these first detected systems will look like and how observations can be optimized to find them and enable electromagnetic follow-up.
AI.method: The authors simulate populations of supermassive black hole binaries constrained by the gravitational-wave background signal, then identify the loudest (most detectable) binary in each simulation to infer the expected properties of the first individually resolvable systems. They systematically explore how detection probability depends on observing strategy parameters, including timing precision (current vs. improved by 2x) and cadence (current vs. increased by 4x), along with combinations of both improvements.

title: Laplace surface of eccentric orbits around Kerr black hole and black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles
summary: We study the Laplace surface of eccentric orbits around a Kerr black hole with a companion star. The two relativistic effects (periapsis apsidal precession and Lense-Thirring precession) balance companion's tidal effect. By solving the secular equations, we find that the two branches of equilibrium solutions exist only in a narrow range of orbital inclinations of test particle, and that the stability exists when companion's obliquity approaches 90 degree. We then study the black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles. In addition to the black-hole suppression on cycle amplitude, we find that the cycle frequency is non-monotonic about distance from black hole and reaches its minimum in the transition between GR apsidal precession and companions's tidal precession. Finally we use this mechanism to well interpret the nearly isotropic orientation of S-cluster in the Galactic center.

Two equilibrium branches exist only in a narrow range of orbital inclinations, with stability achieved when companion obliquity approaches 90 degrees. The study also examines black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles, finding that cycle frequency is non-monotonic with distance from the black hole, reaching a minimum at the transition between GR apsidal precession and companion tidal precession. The mechanism is applied to interpret the nearly isotropic orientation of the S-cluster in the Galactic center.
AI.motivation: To understand how relativistic effects from a Kerr black hole combine with a companion star's tidal influence to shape orbital dynamics, and to explain the observed isotropic orientation of the S-cluster in the Galactic center.
AI.method: The authors solve secular equations governing the Laplace surface for eccentric orbits around a Kerr black hole with a companion star, balancing relativistic precession (apsidal and Lense-Thirring) against the companion's tidal torque. They analyze equilibrium solutions and their stability, and study how black-hole effects modify Lidov-Kozai cycles.

AI.conclusion: Relativistic precession effects from a Kerr black hole, in balance with a companion's tidal influence, produce a limited window of stable Laplace-surface solutions. title: Dynamics and Spectra-Polarimetric Signatures of GRMHD Simulations with Multiple Magnetic Loops
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Relativistic jets are a common outcome of accretion onto black holes, yet their presence and variability depend strongly on the magnetic and dynamical state of the accretion flow. While some systems, such as Blazars and Quasars, launch powerful persistent jets, others, including the Galactic Centre black hole Sgr~A$^\star$, show only weak or transient outflows. The physical conditions leading to the onset or suppression of jet activity remain poorly understood. We investigate the accretion flow conditions that produce transient jets or inhibit jet formation, aiming to improve our understanding of black holes that accrete without strong, steady outflows. We further predict observational signatures in total and polarized emission for comparison with recent observations of Sgr~A$^\star$ in the quiescent state from the radio to the $γ$-ray regime. We perform three-dimensional GRMHD simulations of an accreting black hole surrounded by a torus threaded by a poloidal multi-loop magnetic field of alternating polarities. We follow the evolution of the accretion rate, magnetic flux, and jet power, and analyze angular momentum transport. In addition, radiative transfer calculations including Compton scattering are used to derive synthetic total and polarized emission. The simulations show strong variability in jet power while the initial magnetic polarity loops accrete, followed by weaker activity at later times as the system approaches a semi-MAD state. The emission from the disk is relatively stable, weakly polarized and consistent with the quiet state values reported for SgrA$^\star$. The resulting jet emission is strongly suppressed, depolarized by Faraday rotation and conversion in the surrounding cold plasma. Upscattering calculations yield near-infrared (NIR) high energy light curves that respect observational constraints of the quiescent NIR and X-ray fluxes in SgrA$^\star$

AI.tldr: This paper uses 3D GRMHD simulations of black hole accretion with a multi-loop poloidal magnetic field to show that alternating magnetic polarity leads to suppressed and variable jets, and through radiative transfer calculations, predictions match quiescent Sgr A* observations from radio to gamma-ray.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical conditions that lead to transient jets or suppress jet formation, particularly for black holes like Sgr A* that accrete without strong steady outflows, in contrast to systems like blazars and quasars that launch persistent jets.
AI.method: Three-dimensional GRMHD simulations of an accreting black hole with a torus threaded by a poloidal multi-loop magnetic field of alternating polarities; tracking of accretion rate, magnetic flux, jet power, and angular momentum transport; radiative transfer calculations including Compton scattering to produce synthetic total and polarized emission and upscattering light curves.
AI.result: Strong variability in jet power during accretion of initial magnetic polarity loops, followed by weaker activity as the system enters a semi-MAD state; disk emission is stable and weakly polarized, consistent with Sgr A* quiescent values; jet emission is suppressed and depolarized by Faraday rotation/conversion; NIR high-energy light curves respect quiescent NIR and X-ray flux constraints.
AI.conclusion: Alternating magnetic polarity loops in the accretion flow naturally explain weak/transient jet activity and quiescent multi-wavelength emission from Sgr A*, providing a physical mechanism for suppressed jet formation in certain accreting black holes.

title: Recovering the effective impact parameters in integral-field absorption-line tomography
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy of extended background sources, such as gravitational arcs, delivers many closely spaced absorption sightlines through the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of foreground galaxies. However, the source extent and smearing through the point spread function (PSF) cause each spaxel to integrate light from a region larger than itself. The usually adopted geometric spaxel centre is therefore not representative of where the absorbed flux originates. Informed by high-resolution imaging, we introduce a flux-contribution formalism that reconstructs the spatial origin of the flux in each spaxel by defining flux-weighted coordinates and impact parameters. Using a data-driven simulation built on a real gravitational-arc configuration, we show that spaxel centres are displaced from the flux-weighted positions by $|Δ\mathbf{x}| \propto θ_{\rm PSF}(1-f)$, with $f$ the spaxel-source overlap fraction, and that the resulting impact-parameter bias scales with the lensing magnification as $μ^{-1/2}$. These offsets are largest for off-arc spaxels and flatten the radial column-density profiles. They also inject a coherent geometry-driven scatter that mimics intrinsic CGM structure and that is removed neither by a tighter spaxel selection nor by a finer spatial binning. For identical uncertainties, the spaxel-centre coordinates leave residuals of about twice the noise level ($χ^2_ν\sim 4$), whereas the flux-weighted coordinates recover the input profile to within the uncertainties ($χ^2_ν\sim 1$) and remain robust to a PSF misspecification of $\pm 10\%$. The method we propose provides a better-motivated and readily adoptable framework for tomographic studies, whether as the primary analysis or as a robustness check on spaxel-centre results.

The authors develop a flux-contribution formalism using flux-weighted coordinates and impact parameters informed by high-resolution imaging, demonstrating that spaxel centres are displaced by |Δx| ∝ θ_PSF(1-f) and that impact-parameter bias scales as μ^{-1/2}. They show the spaxel-centre approach leaves residuals about twice the noise level (χ²_ν ~ 4), while the flux-weighted method recovers the input profile within uncertainties (χ²_ν ~ 1) and is robust to ±10% PSF misspecification.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to correct a fundamental methodological flaw in IFU spectroscopy of extended background sources: the commonly assumed geometric spaxel centre does not reflect where absorbed flux actually originates, due to source extent and PSF smearing. This introduces systematic biases in impact-parameter measurements and artificially mimics intrinsic CGM structure, which cannot be removed by tighter spaxel selection or finer binning.

The method remains robust to ±10% PSF misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The proposed flux-contribution framework provides a better-motivated and readily adoptable approach for tomographic CGM studies using IFU spectroscopy of gravitational arcs, suitable either as the primary analysis method or as a robustness check on spaxel-centre-based results.

title: Evidence for a spectral steepening of the gamma-ray emission from the Galactic Center ridge
comment: H.E.S.S. Collaboration
summary: Very-high-energy (VHE) $γ$-ray emission detected from the central molecular zone (CMZ) hints at diffusive propagation of cosmic rays (CRs) injected continuously near the Galactic center (GC). Using H.E.S.S. VHE $γ$-ray observations, we aim to construct a multi-component description of the region in order to derive the spatial and spectral distributions of CRs and discuss their potential origin. We rely on a spectro-morphological analysis, in which spectral and spatial parameters of different components are fit simultaneously, and on a three-dimensional description of the CMZ and CR distributions. The GC ridge emission is well reproduced with the assumed gas distribution model weighted by a $1/r^α$ CR density profile with $α= 1.10 \pm 0.05_{\rm{stat}} \pm 0.10_{\rm{syst}}$. We detect no significant spectral variations across the CMZ, which supports a continuous injection from the GC. We report a significant (> 3 $σ$) curvature in the GC ridge $γ$-ray spectrum, implying a parent proton break (or cutoff energy) of $E_b \sim 15-50$ TeV ($E_{\rm{cut}} \sim 60-160$ TeV). We also derive the best-fit spectral parameters of the other sources in the region and report a significant cutoff at $E \sim 5$ TeV in the spectrum of the pulsar wind nebula G0.9+0.1. Finally we constrain the position of the injection site to be close to the GC (ruling out the Arches and Quintuplet clusters as major contributors to the emission). We discuss possible origins for the GC ridge emission, potential mechanisms for causing the observed curvature, a possible contribution of the gas content to the emission of HESS J1745-290 and derive qualitative constraints on the line-of-sight positions of the clouds shaping the CMZ.

The pulsar wind nebula G0.9+0.1 shows a cutoff at ~5 TeV, and the injection site is constrained to be near the GC, ruling out Arches and Quintuplet clusters as major contributors.

AI.method: A spectro-morphological analysis is employed, simultaneously fitting spectral and spatial parameters of multiple components, combined with a three-dimensional description of the CMZ and cosmic-ray distributions.

Possible origins for the ridge emission, mechanisms for the spectral curvature, and gas contributions to HESS J1745-290 are discussed, along with constraints on line-of-sight cloud positions in the CMZ.

title: Infrared photoprocessing of porous amorphous solid water with a free electron laser
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures in main text, 4 figures in Appendix
summary: Water ice is the most abundant ice in the interstellar medium (ISM). Previous studies on porous amorphous solid water (pASW) have shown that the infrared radiation field in the ISM modeled with infrared free electron laser (FEL) irradiation can result in changes in the ice towards a more ordered structure, characterized by a change in the OH-stretching vibration band. This paper aims to study the restructuring in more detail by varying the irradiation intensity and irradiation time for irradiations on-resonance with the OH-stretching, bending and libration modes. In addition, desorption of H2O is monitored during the irradiations. The research presented in this paper considers 42 infrared FEL irradiations on pASW samples deposited at two different rates, using the infrared FELs of the HFML-FELIX laboratory. Restructuring is studied using reflection absorption infrared (RAIR) spectroscopy, with a mass spectrometer monitoring the desorption of H2O in an ultra-high vacuum system. Desorption and restructuring occur in parallel, with the strongest effects observed for irradiation on-resonance with the OH-stretching vibration. Both processes exhibit two distinct regimes: an initial strong restructuring and desorption, characterized by an exponential decrease in the intensity of the desorption peaks within the first 5 s of irradiation, followed by a second regime of less efficient, yet continued restructuring and constant desorption in an extended area, involving energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. The trends in restructuring and desorption, depending on the absorbed energy during irradiation, are significantly different, suggesting separate processes. The astrophysical relevance of in particular the second regime of constant desorption and restructuring is discussed.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the restructuring and desorption of porous amorphous solid water (pASW) induced by infrared free electron laser (FEL) irradiation at various intensities and times, on-resonance with OH-stretching, bending, and libration modes. Using 42 irradiations at the HFML-FELIX laboratory, the authors find that both restructuring and desorption occur in parallel, strongest on OH-stretching resonance, and exhibit two regimes: an initial rapid exponential phase (within 5 s) followed by a slower, sustained phase involving energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. The distinct trends for restructuring versus desorption suggest separate underlying processes, with astrophysical implications particularly for the second regime.
AI.motivation: To understand how the interstellar infrared radiation field modifies porous amorphous solid water ice, specifically characterizing the intensity and time dependence of irradiation-induced restructuring and desorption, and to determine whether these processes are linked or independent.
AI.method: 42 infrared FEL irradiations were performed on pASW samples deposited at two different rates, using the HFML-FELIX facility. Irradiations were tuned to OH-stretching, bending, and libration modes at varying intensities and durations. Restructuring was monitored via reflection absorption infrared (RAIR) spectroscopy, while H2O desorption was tracked with a mass spectrometer in an ultra-high vacuum system.
AI.result: Restructuring and desorption occur simultaneously, strongest when irradiation is on-resonance with the OH-stretching vibration. Both processes show two regimes: an initial strong response with exponential decay of desorption peak intensity within the first 5 seconds, followed by a second regime of less efficient but sustained restructuring and constant desorption, attributed to energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. The restructuring and desorption trends differ significantly as a function of absorbed energy, indicating they are separate processes.
AI.conclusion: The irradiation-induced restructuring and desorption of pASW are distinct but parallel processes, each displaying a two-regime behavior. The second regime of constant desorption and restructuring is particularly relevant for astrophysical environments, where sustained ice processing occurs over long timescales in the interstellar medium.

title: Winds Against Alignment: AGN Feedback and the Spin Evolution of Massive Black Hole Binaries
summary: The interaction between massive black hole (MBH) binaries and circumbinary discs (CBDs) affects the spin orientations of merging binaries - a key observable for the future LISA mission. While gas accretion is known to align BH spins with the orbital angular momentum via the Bardeen-Petterson effect, the impact of AGN feedback on this process has remained largely unexplored. We present hydrodynamical simulations of an equal-mass MBH binary embedded in a CBD, using the GIZMO code with a subgrid model that self-consistently evolves BH mass, spin, and anisotropic AGN feedback. We explore different BH spin magnitudes and orientations to identify the configurations producing the strongest feedback effect on the disc structure and binary evolution. AGN winds substantially modify the CBD and minidisc structure, enlarging the central cavity and, after 20-25 binary orbits, destroying the minidiscs in all feedback simulations. Feedback-driven cavity excavation suppresses the gravitational torques driving orbital evolution, causing the binary to stall. AGN feedback dramatically affects MBH accretion, reducing the Eddington ratio by one to two orders of magnitude before ultimately suppressing it entirely. This strongly inhibits Bardeen-Petterson spin alignment, delaying it well beyond the feedback-free timescale. Extending one simulation to 70 binary orbits reveals a feedback-regulated duty cycle of alternating active and quiescent phases, with the binary spending most of its time in low-density, quiescent conditions that further suppress alignment. These results indicate that AGN feedback is an important, previously overlooked channel for preserving spin misalignment in MBH binaries prior to coalescence, with direct implications for interpreting LISA gravitational-wave observations.

AI.motivation: The spin orientations of merging MBH binaries are a key observable for LISA. While gas accretion is known to align BH spins with orbital angular momentum via the Bardeen-Petterson effect, the impact of AGN feedback on this process has remained largely unexplored — this study fills that gap.
AI.method: The authors use the GIZMO code to run hydrodynamical simulations of an equal-mass MBH binary embedded in a CBD, incorporating a subgrid model that self-consistently evolves BH mass, spin, and anisotropic AGN feedback. They explore different BH spin magnitudes and orientations to identify configurations producing the strongest feedback effects on disc structure and binary evolution, extending one simulation to 70 binary orbits to examine long-term behavior.

Feedback-driven cavity excavation suppresses gravitational torques, causing the binary to stall. AGN feedback reduces the Eddington ratio by one to two orders of magnitude before suppressing it entirely, strongly inhibiting Bardeen-Petterson spin alignment. The extended 70-orbit simulation reveals a feedback-regulated duty cycle with alternating active and quiescent phases, with the binary spending most time in low-density quiescent conditions that further suppress alignment.
AI.conclusion: AGN feedback is an important, previously overlooked channel for preserving spin misalignment in MBH binaries prior to coalescence, with direct implications for interpreting LISA gravitational-wave observations.

title: Energetics of AGN Feedback
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables; accepted in MNRAS
summary: Integrating realistic active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback into cosmological hydrodynamical simulations remains a major challenge as resolving the spatial coupling of jet energy over cosmic timescales is computationally prohibitive. We present an analytic framework that predicts the radial and polar-angle dependence of feedback energy from lobed AGNs, enabling a physically motivated, computationally efficient prescription for jet feedback. Built upon the Radio AGN in Semi-analytic Environments (RAiSE) dynamical model, our approach tracks the post-AGN jet phase evolution of radio sources through two distinct mechanisms: buoyantly rising bubbles subject to ablation, and the gravitational collapse of swept-up gas in the shocked shell. We find that these two feedback mechanisms produce strongly contrasting spatial distributions across ten representative cluster environments. Buoyant bubbles preferentially deposit energy in steep density gradients near the core radius, while the collapsing shocked gas shell drives heating within flatter cluster cores. Weak, short-lived AGN outbursts ($Q<10^{37}$ W and $t_{\rm on}<10$ Myr) confine their energy deposition to the inner 10 kpc of the cluster; longer-lived events ($t_{\rm on} \geqslant 100$ Myr) deposit less than 1% of their injected energy within 30 kpc. We find that time-averaged heating rates across multiple outbursts are sufficient to offset radiative cooling in all but the highest density cluster cores (within 100 kpc) for duty cycles of $0.08< δ\leqslant 1$. This framework provides a scalable basis for modelling anisotropic, physically motivated jet feedback that can be incorporated into next-generation cosmological simulations.

The framework shows these mechanisms produce contrasting spatial energy distributions in cluster environments, with weak/short outbursts confined to inner regions, and demonstrates that time-averaged heating can offset radiative cooling in all but the densest cluster cores for certain duty cycles.

The authors seek to develop a computationally efficient but physically motivated prescription for jet feedback.
AI.method: The framework is built upon the RAiSE (Radio AGN in Semi-analytic Environments) dynamical model, tracking post-AGN jet phase evolution through two distinct mechanisms: (1) buoyantly rising bubbles subject to ablation, and (2) gravitational collapse of swept-up gas in the shocked shell. The framework predicts radial and polar-angle dependence of feedback energy, tested across ten representative cluster environments with varying outburst properties (jet power Q and active timescale t_on).

title: Particle acceleration in Alfvénic turbulence with a strong guide field
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures
summary: Magnetically dominated Alfvénic turbulence creates an effective environment for particle acceleration. However, when a strong mean field is present, traditional mechanisms like mirror and curvature acceleration become inefficient at explaining non-thermal particle energy distributions. Based on numerical and phenomenological study, we propose that in such turbulence, particles are accelerated in charge-starved current sheets, corresponding to current velocities approaching the speed of light. The distributions of the electric currents, plasma density, fluctuations of electric charge, as well as the energy distributions of accelerated particles, approximately follow log-normal statistics. Non-thermal particle distributions thus arise from particle acceleration in these charge-starved current sheets rather than from conventional Fermi-type particle acceleration by turbulent eddies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that in magnetically dominated Alfvénic turbulence with a strong mean field, particle acceleration occurs in charge-starved current sheets where current velocities approach the speed of light, rather than through traditional Fermi-type mechanisms. Key physical quantities follow log-normal statistics, explaining non-thermal particle energy distributions.
AI.motivation: Traditional particle acceleration mechanisms like mirror and curvature acceleration become inefficient in magnetically dominated Alfvénic turbulence with a strong mean field, yet non-thermal particle distributions are still observed. This creates a need for an alternative acceleration mechanism.
AI.method: The study combines numerical simulations with phenomenological analysis to examine electric current distributions, plasma density fluctuations, electric charge fluctuations, and the resulting energy distributions of accelerated particles in magnetically dominated Alfvénic turbulence.
AI.result: The paper finds that particle acceleration occurs in charge-starved current sheets, where current velocities approach the speed of light. The distributions of electric currents, plasma density, charge fluctuations, and accelerated particle energies all approximately follow log-normal statistics.
AI.conclusion: Non-thermal particle distributions in magnetically dominated Alfvénic turbulence arise from particle acceleration in charge-starved current sheets, not from conventional Fermi-type acceleration by turbulent eddies.

title: The Nobeyama 45 m Survey of Shocked Molecular Gas in the Central Molecular Zone. I. Survey Data, Cloud Catalog, and SiO Line-Ratio Trends
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJS. 36 pages, 27 figures, 4 tables. Calibrated FITS data products are available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.19588616
summary: We present large-scale molecular line maps of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in our Galaxy obtained with the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45 m telescope. The observations cover a 3.5 deg x 0.5 deg region with 20 arcsec resolution in eight molecular lines including SiO J=2-1, CS J=2-1, H13CN J=1-0, and HCN J=1-0. We release the calibrated data cubes and a catalog of SiO-emitting clouds identified by the SCIMES algorithm. For each cloud, we provide cloud-integrated intensities of the observed lines and derive an H13CN-based molecular gas mass and a cloud-averaged H2 number density. We compare SiO intensity ratios with the density, dynamical time, and their product n_H2 t_dyn. We find that SiO intensity ratios relative to six other molecular lines all decrease systematically with increasing n_H2 t_dyn. The tightest correlations are found for SiO/H13CN (r_s = -0.82) and SiO/CS (r_s = -0.70). The released data cubes and cloud catalog enable systematic studies of SiO enhancement, shock chemistry, and gas dynamical evolution across the CMZ.

The authors release calibrated data cubes and a catalog of SiO-emitting clouds identified with SCIMES, providing cloud-integrated intensities, H13CN-based masses, and cloud-averaged H2 densities. They find that SiO intensity ratios relative to six other lines systematically decrease with increasing n_H2 t_dyn, with the tightest correlations for SiO/H13CN (r_s = -0.82) and SiO/CS (r_s = -0.70), enabling systematic studies of SiO enhancement and shock chemistry in the CMZ.

title: Finding and using interpretable latents in a neutrino foundation model with sparse autoencoders
summary: We present a first application of sparse-autoencoder-based mechanistic interpretability to particle physics. Studying a neutrino foundation model pretrained on IceCube data and fine-tuned for direction reconstruction, we identify a validated atlas of physical concepts in the model representation, using a strict validation protocol consisting of held-out tests, matched nuisance controls, and replication across independent dictionary trainings. Causal interventions show that the direction head barely draws on this atlas. Motivated by this underused information, we train an uncertainty head on the same event-level representation to predict the model's angular reconstruction error. Unlike the direction head, it depends causally on quality and brightness features from the atlas. At $20\%$ selection efficiency, this interpretable estimator improves the median angular resolution from $20.2^\circ$ to $3.2^\circ$. These results suggest that mechanistic interpretability can reveal learned latent physics encoded within a model's internal representation and help design downstream tasks that exploit it.

AI.tldr: The paper applies sparse-autoencoder-based mechanistic interpretability to a neutrino foundation model pretrained on IceCube data. It identifies a validated atlas of physical concepts in the model's internal representation, shows the direction-reconstruction head barely uses these concepts, and trains an interpretable uncertainty head on the same representation that predicts angular reconstruction error. This improves median angular resolution from 20.2° to 3.2° at 20% selection efficiency.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that mechanistic interpretability can reveal learned latent physics in model internals and inform the design of downstream tasks that exploit this information, beyond what the original task head uses.
AI.method: Apply sparse autoencoders to the internal representation of a neutrino foundation model (pretrained on IceCube data, fine-tuned for direction reconstruction). Validate discovered features via a strict protocol: held-out tests, matched nuisance controls, and replication across independent dictionary trainings. Perform causal interventions to assess feature usage by the direction head, then train an uncertainty head on the same representation to predict angular reconstruction error.
AI.result: The direction head barely uses the identified concept atlas, while the uncertainty head causally depends on quality and brightness features. At 20% selection efficiency, the interpretable estimator improves median angular resolution from 20.2° to 3.2°.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can uncover learned latent physics encoded in model internals and guide downstream task design to exploit underused information, suggesting broader applications of this approach in physics.

title: Revealing Galactic dust beneath the cosmic infrared background anisotropies with Wavelet Phase Harmonics
comment: 20 pages, 20 figures
summary: Separating Galactic dust emission from cosmic infrared background (CIB) anisotropies is challenging because both the emission components have similar spectral properties. The primary objective of this work is to develop a component-separation algorithm to extract the Galactic dust emission from CIB anisotropies dominated sky regions using Wavelet Phase Harmonics statistics (WPH). We apply our algorithm to the \textit{Planck} $353\,\mathrm{GHz}$ frequency band over three sky regions spanning a range of neutral hydrogen ($\text{HI}$) column densities at high Galactic latitudes. In all three regions, we successfully recover the dust signal without significant leakage between the dust and CIB anisotropy components. We use the low signal-to-noise ($\mathrm{S/N}$) region to validate the component-separation algorithm and compare its performance with the standard template-fit approach that uses the linear dust-$\text{HI}$ correlation relation. For intermediate and high $\mathrm{S/N}$ regions, we separate the dust signal map from the contamination while preserving the statistical correlation with $\text{HI}$ column density map. Dust maps are used to analyze the relationship between dust and $\text{HI}$ emissions. We characterize the spatial variations in dust emission relative to the hydrogen column density as a function of the angular scale.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a component-separation algorithm using Wavelet Phase Harmonics (WPH) statistics to extract Galactic dust emission from cosmic infrared background (CIB) anisotropies in Planck 353 GHz data across three high-latitude sky regions with varying HI column densities. The method successfully recovers dust signals without leakage between components and is validated against a standard template-fit approach.
AI.motivation: Separating Galactic dust emission from CIB anisotropies is difficult because both components exhibit similar spectral properties. A robust component-separation algorithm is needed to extract Galactic dust from CIB-dominated sky regions for accurate analysis of dust-HI correlations and spatial variations.
AI.method: The algorithm leverages Wavelet Phase Harmonics (WPH) statistics for component separation. It is applied to Planck 353 GHz data over three sky regions spanning a range of HI column densities at high Galactic latitudes. The low signal-to-noise region is used for validation against the standard template-fit method based on linear dust-HI correlation, while intermediate and high S/N regions are used to separate dust signal maps while preserving statistical correlation with HI column density.
